assessment.nobel_worthiness: Technology, tasks and trade shocks as drivers of labour demand and wage inequality. The work changed how economists and policymakers think about who gains and loses from technological change and globalisation. The empirical designs are transparent and the findings have been widely examined, including by replication and robustness work.
assessment.attribution: Katz's work with Autor on skill demand and the education-technology race, Autor's task framework, and the Autor-Dorn-Hanson China-shock papers form a coherent set. Dorn is omitted to keep the group to three, and the task-model theory is shared with other scholars outside this entry, so the boundaries are somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of evidence, with the China-shock results tested and refined for roughly ten years. Policy relevance is high and the topic is timely.
uncertainties: Some of the China-shock magnitudes and the longer-run effects remain debated.
Overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes on technology and growth, and with Acemoglu's task-based work, may affect how the committee weighs this entry.
Dorn is excluded by the three-name limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The foundation of modern monetary policy analysis: staggered nominal price setting, policy rules and the New Keynesian framework used in central banks. The theory is influential and the practical impact is large.
assessment.attribution: The credited list is very large (eight names). Calvo supplies the pricing mechanism, Taylor the policy rule and Woodford the integrated framework. Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, Smets and others also made major contributions, so any trio will leave out important co-contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and tested over decades. The 2022 prize for banking and financial crises is adjacent and the 2011 prize is related, so there is some risk of macro crowding.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested and the choice of three from eight is difficult.
Whether the committee sees the framework as sufficiently validated after the 2008 and post-2020 episodes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed international trade by moving the focus from industries to firms and by identifying new channels for gains from trade. It is a large paradigm shift with extensive empirical follow-up using firm-level data.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central paper, and Helpman's broader work on trade with increasing returns and heterogeneous firms underpins the field. Redding, Bernard, Eaton and Kortum have related contributions, and this list shares credit with the quantitative trade entry (B042).
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation and extension. The key predictions are broadly supported, though not uniformly.
uncertainties: Whether Krugman's 2008 prize is seen as already covering the new-trade-theory lineage.
Credit division among Melitz, Bernard-Jensen-Eaton-Kortum, Helpman and Redding.
Some structural implications depend on functional-form assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design gave a new tractable framework for how an informed party optimally shapes others' information. It has been applied in many areas, including regulation, matching and platforms.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica-Gentzkow (2011) is the origin. Bergemann-Morris developed the related Bayes correlated equilibrium and information-design theory. Gentzkow's other empirical work is not part of this entry. Choosing three leaves out Bergemann, which is a real attribution difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Relatively recent, about fifteen years, with rapid theoretical growth but limited direct empirical validation.
uncertainties: The framework may be judged too young, and applied evidence is thin.
Contested credit among four plausible names.
Overlap with the information-economics and mechanism-design prizes (2007, 2020, 2016).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data was used to measure intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation, and quasi-experimental designs were used to study neighbourhood effects. It changed how mobility is measured and debated, and has had large policy and research impact.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear central figure, with Hendren a leading contributor on place effects and Friedman and Katz also prominent. Large teams make precise attribution difficult. Chetty also has separate contributions on taxation and behavioural public economics.
assessment.maturity: About a decade of work. Core descriptive facts have held up well, while some causal place-effect estimates are still being refined and are open to replication scrutiny.
uncertainties: Maturity, including debate on the neighbourhood-effect estimates.
Division of credit within a large team and with earlier mobility scholars such as Solon and Corak.
Whether a prize here would be seen as too early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resource misallocation across firms was established as a quantitatively important source of cross-country income differences. It provides a measurement-based link between micro frictions and aggregate productivity, and has influenced growth and development research.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the key paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is an independent parallel contribution, so excluding Restuccia is a real attribution problem.
assessment.maturity: Well-established and heavily cited, but the quantitative magnitudes depend on measurement choices that are still debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error in firm-level productivity may inflate estimated misallocation.
Credit division with Restuccia and Rogerson.
Relation to the 2025 growth prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Social preferences, meaning reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion, established through laboratory and field evidence that many people depart from pure self-interest in systematic ways. This shaped behavioural, contract and public economics. The experimental findings have replicated reasonably well, though effect sizes vary with context.
assessment.attribution: Fehr-Schmidt (1999) provides the formal model, and Fehr's wider experimental programme (including with Gächter) provides much of the evidence. Falk is also credited, and Bolton-Ockenfels and Rabin made contributions that are not listed here. I have a general familiarity with this literature, and no direct co-authorship link with these individuals is disclosed in my profile.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with 25 years of replication and extension. Some debate remains about how far lab-based preferences generalise to field behaviour and about the stability of specific parameters.
uncertainties: External validity beyond lab and stylised games.
Overlap with the 2017 behavioural prize and the 2002 prize for experimental methods.
Credit among Fehr, Gächter, Falk, Bolton and Ockenfels, and Rabin.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators (Arellano-Bond, Arellano-Bover, Blundell-Bond) became standard tools for applied economics with panel data. This is a major methodological contribution used across subfields, and methods Nobels of this type, such as the 2021 prize for causal inference, have a clear precedent.
assessment.attribution: Credit is clear for the core estimators, with Arellano-Bond (1991) and Blundell-Bond (1998) as the key papers. Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen, Anderson-Hsiao and Hansen's GMM are earlier foundations, and Hansen's 2013 prize covers GMM.
assessment.maturity: Mature and highly used. Known weaknesses, including proliferation of instruments and weak-instrument problems, have become well documented. That is useful in itself, since much applied use has been mechanical.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with Hansen's GMM prize.
Applied misuse and fragility in many applications may weaken the case.
Blundell has other substantial contributions, such as on labour supply and consumption, that might also be considered separately.
